argv:
You generate synthetic meeting transcripts with gold annotations for LiveMinutes, a research dataset modeled on the AMI Meeting Corpus scenario meetings.

In AMI scenario meetings, a team of four plays a design team in a fictional company. The roles are Project Manager (PM), Marketing Expert (ME), User Interface designer (UI) and Industrial Designer (ID). A series has four meetings: (a) kickoff, (b) functional design, (c) conceptual design, (d) detailed design. Later meetings refer back to earlier ones.

Write natural spoken conversation the way AMI transcripts read: short turns, fillers ("um", "uh", "yeah"), backchannels ("mm-hmm", "okay"), interruptions, people building on each other, and some disfluency. Do not write a screenplay. Do not narrate. No stage directions.

Each segment is one dialogue-act-like unit: one speaker, usually one clause or short sentence, sometimes just a backchannel. Give each segment an AMI dialogue-act type from this set:
  bck backchannel, stl stall, fra fragment, inf inform, sug suggest, ass assess,
  el.inf elicit-inform, el.sug elicit-offer-or-suggestion, el.ass elicit-assessment,
  el.und elicit-comment-understanding, off offer, und comment-about-understanding,
  be.pos be-positive, be.neg be-negative, oth other

Absent participants NEVER speak. Speaker labels are ground truth: use only the labels you are given.

The gold annotations must be exactly true of the transcript you write. Refer to segments by their "n" number. Every number you cite must exist.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else: no prose, no markdown fences.

request.user:
Write meeting SY0207c: meeting "c" (conceptual design) of series SY0207.

PROJECT
The team is designing a voice-controlled kitchen timer.

PARTICIPANTS (label, role, status for this meeting)
A  User Interface designer (UI)  Priya  ABSENT, never speaks
B  Project Manager (PM)  Martin  present
C  Industrial Designer (ID)  Sofie  present
D  Marketing Expert (ME)  Gareth  present

EARLIER MEETINGS IN THIS SERIES
Stay consistent with them. Refer back to them, follow up on their open action items, and keep the same product and team.

[SY0207a, kickoff]
  abstract: The project manager opened the kickoff meeting, noted that the user interface designer was absent, and had the industrial designer and marketing expert introduce themselves. He presented the project, a voice-controlled kitchen timer, and explained the series of four meetings, after which the team practised with the whiteboard. He gave the financial targets: a selling price of 25 euros, a maximum production cost of 12.50 euros per unit including the voice components, and a profit aim of 50 million euros for the international market. The team raised concerns that voice recognition chips could strain the budget and that an international market implies multiple languages. In the initial brainstorm the team agreed on multiple named timers and voice-first control with a physical stop button as backup; a phone app was suggested but set aside, and battery versus mains power was left open.
  decisions: The timer will support multiple named timers. The timer will be voice-first, with a physical stop button as backup.
  actions: The industrial designer will investigate the working design: components, power source, microphone and speaker. The marketing expert will research user requirements through a small survey and a review of existing kitchen timers. The user interface designer, though absent, was assigned to design the voice commands and the timer's spoken responses. The project manager will email the user interface designer the brief and her assignment. Checking the cost of voice recognition chips was mentioned but nobody took it on.
  problems: The cost of voice recognition chips is unknown and may be hard to fit within the 12.50 euro production cost; no one is responsible for checking it. Selling internationally means the voice control may need to support several languages. Battery versus mains power is undecided; the industrial designer leans towards battery. The idea of a phone app was parked and not resolved.
  action item SY0207a.ai1: Investigate the working design: required components, power source (battery or plug), microphone and speaker. (owner C, active)
  action item SY0207a.ai2: Research user requirements for kitchen timers via a survey and a review of existing products. (owner D, active)
  action item SY0207a.ai3: Design the voice command interface: what the commands are and what the timer says back. (owner A, active)
  action item SY0207a.ai4: Email the user interface designer the project brief and her assignment. (owner B, active)
  action item SY0207a.ai5: Check the cost of voice recognition chips. (owner no owner, active)
  fact (absence): Priya, the user interface designer (A), was absent from the kickoff meeting.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert suggested connecting the timer to a phone app; the idea was parked over cost concerns.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The industrial designer leaned towards battery power, but battery versus plug-in was not decided.

[SY0207b, functional design]
  abstract: The project manager opened the functional design meeting with the full team present, confirmed that the user interface designer had received the brief by email, and recapped the kickoff decisions on multiple named timers and voice-first control with a physical stop button. The industrial designer presented the working design: a microphone, a small speaker, a voice recognition chip, a button and battery power, and she noted that an always-listening microphone with a wake word could drain AA batteries within a couple of months and that the chip's price is still unknown. The marketing expert reported a survey of about forty people: users dislike touching timers with dirty hands, often run several dishes at once and want three or four timers, need a loud alarm, and rarely want an app; voice competitors are expensive smart speakers, while simple timers sell for 5 to 15 euros. The user interface designer presented a small fixed command set with a wake word, short spoken confirmations, a fixed list of timer names plus numbered timers, and alarms that announce the timer's name. The team agreed on battery power, up to four named timers, the fixed command set, named spoken alarms, and dropping the phone app; a screen and the choice of languages remain open.
  decisions: The timer will be battery powered. The timer will support up to four named timers. Voice control will use a small fixed command set with a fixed list of timer names plus numbered timers. When a timer finishes, the alarm will loudly announce the timer's name. The phone app idea is dropped for good.
  actions: The industrial designer will check the cost of voice recognition chips; the marketing expert first offered to do this, but the industrial designer took it because she is already pricing the components. The industrial designer will estimate battery life with the always-listening wake word. The user interface designer will write out the full voice command list and all spoken responses. The marketing expert will find out which markets matter most and which languages to prioritise. The project manager will send round the minutes. The user interface designer was first asked to research whether competing timers offer app connectivity, but this task was dropped once the team decided against an app.
  problems: The cost of the voice recognition chip is still unknown. Battery life with an always-listening microphone may be short. The marketing expert proposed a small screen to show the timers; the industrial designer and user interface designer raised cost, battery and hands-free concerns, and the question was left open. It is not yet decided which languages to support at launch, and each language needs its own word list and voice recordings. The speaker must be loud enough to be heard over an extractor fan.
  action item SY0207b.ai1: Check the cost of voice recognition chips (full speech versus fixed vocabulary). (owner C, active)
  action item SY0207b.ai2: Research whether competing kitchen timers offer phone app connectivity. (owner A, dropped)
  action item SY0207b.ai3: Write out the full voice command list and all of the timer's spoken responses. (owner A, active)
  action item SY0207b.ai4: Find out which markets matter most and which languages to prioritise. (owner D, active)
  action item SY0207b.ai5: Estimate battery life with the always-listening wake word. (owner C, active)
  action item SY0207b.ai6: Send round the meeting minutes. (owner B, active)
  fact (plan_change): The phone app, which had been parked at the kickoff, was finally dropped in this meeting.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert proposed a small screen to show the timers; the industrial designer and user interface designer raised concerns, and the project manager left it open.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The user interface designer suggested launching in English plus a couple of other languages, but the languages were not decided.
  fact (action_item_removed): The user interface designer's task to research competitor app connectivity was dropped after the team decided against an app.

EDGE CASES THIS MEETING MUST CONTAIN
Weave each one naturally into the project discussion. Each must be clearly present, and each must be tagged with the segments where it happens.
- F2_VAGUE_NO_OWNER [F2]: A task is mentioned vaguely ("someone should probably check the costs") and no one takes it. The gold action item has owner null and owner_unclear true.
  Required gold labels: action_items, edge_cases.
- F2_TASK_TO_ABSENT [F2]: A task is assigned to a team member who is absent from this meeting. The gold action item owner is that absent participant.
  Required gold labels: action_items, edge_cases.

LENGTH
Between 90 and 140 segments.

GOLD LABELS
- summary: AMI-style abstractive summary in third person, using role names ("The project manager ..."). Sections: abstract (3-6 sentences), actions, decisions, problems (open issues). It reflects the meeting's FINAL state: corrected values, final plans, and no jokes or tangents reported as content.
- action_items: every task arising in the meeting. owner is the speaker label of the FINAL owner, and may be an absent participant. owner is null ONLY for a task nobody takes, with owner_unclear true. status is the final status: active, reassigned (owner changed; previous_owners lists earlier owners) or dropped. history lists the events in order. evidence_segments lists the supporting segments.
- qa_facts: atomic facts someone could later ask about ("Who was asked to ...?", "Did the team agree on ...?"). Include every decision (agreed true), every proposal nobody agreed to (type unagreed_proposal, agreed false), action items, removed action items, absences, and plan changes. Because this meeting follows earlier ones, include at least one fact of type reference_to_prior_meeting, with refers_to_meeting set, at a point where someone refers back to an earlier meeting. Do NOT write questions.
- edge_cases: one entry per edge case above, with its scenario_id and the segment numbers that contain it.

OUTPUT JSON SHAPE
{
  "segments": [{"n": 1, "speaker": "A", "da_type": "inf", "text": "..."}],
  "summary": {"abstract": ["..."], "actions": ["..."], "decisions": ["..."], "problems": ["..."]},
  "action_items": [{"n": 1, "description": "...", "owner": "C", "owner_unclear": false, "status": "active", "previous_owners": [], "history": [{"segment": 12, "event": "assigned", "by": "A", "owner": "C"}], "evidence_segments": [12, 13]}],
  "qa_facts": [{"type": "decision", "fact": "...", "agreed": true, "related_action_item": null, "refers_to_meeting": null, "evidence_segments": [40]}],
  "edge_cases": [{"scenario_id": "...", "segments": [20, 21, 22], "note": "one line on how it appears"}]
}
history events: proposed, offered, assigned, accepted, reassigned, dropped, restated. qa_facts types: decision, unagreed_proposal, action_item, action_item_removed, absence, plan_change, reference_to_prior_meeting, other. related_action_item is an action item's "n" or null. refers_to_meeting is an earlier meeting ID of this series or null.
